paragraphs.heading: Exploring the sea
paragraphs.text: Ocean exploration is the part of oceanography concerned with exploring the oceans' surfaces. It moved forward together with advances in shipbuilding, diving, navigation, depth measurement and mapmaking. Many peoples made notable voyages, among them the Greeks, Phoenicians, Romans, Polynesians, Vikings, Arabs and Portuguese. Scientific investigation began with early scientists such as Edmund Halley, James Cook and Charles Darwin.

paragraphs.heading: Early sailors
paragraphs.text: People began diving into the sea around 4500 BC, for food, trade and possibly warfare. By about 4000 BC Egyptians had built sailing vessels, which were probably sailed only in the eastern Mediterranean, close to where the Nile meets the sea. Polynesians settled the islands of the South Pacific between 4000 BC and 1000 AD. Around 600 BC the Phoenicians opened sea routes across the whole Mediterranean and into the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. They knew how to navigate by the stars but probably kept land in sight when they could.

paragraphs.heading: Finding your place
paragraphs.text: Greek traders between 500 and 200 BC estimated latitude from how long the day lasted, adjusted for the season. Around 325 BC the Greek astronomer Pytheas sailed north out of the Mediterranean, reaching England and perhaps Iceland and Norway. He also developed sightings of the North Star as a way to find latitude. About 240 BC Eratosthenes of Cyrene measured the Earth's circumference with high precision. Between 1768 and 1780, James Cook searched the southern oceans for a southern continent and was the first to fix longitude with a marine chronometer.

paragraphs.heading: Long voyages
paragraphs.text: Vikings explored and settled Iceland, Greenland and Newfoundland between 900 and 1430, and Leif Erikson reached North America in 1002. From 1405 to 1433 China sent seven voyages to spread its influence and impress neighbouring states, but these costly trips were ended after a short time. Ferdinand Magellan's ships sailed all the way around the world between 1519 and 1522.

paragraphs.heading: Science at sea
paragraphs.text: Edmund Halley's voyage of 1698 to 1700 was probably the first made mainly for science. He studied how the magnetic compass varies and sailed as far as 52 degrees south in the Atlantic. Charles Darwin sailed on the Beagle from 1831 to 1836, exploring the Galapagos and many other places, and this work led him to the ideas of natural selection and evolution. The Challenger travelled the globe on a scientific mission, collecting sediment and water samples, soundings and many biological specimens.

paragraphs.heading: Going deeper
paragraphs.text: In 1620 the Dutch inventor Cornelis Drebbel built the world's first submarine and took it on several trips in the River Thames, around 12 to 15 feet down. In 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste dived to what was then believed to be the deepest point of the Mariana Trench, observing a depth of 10,915 meters. In 1969 the Ben Franklin drifted underwater in the Gulf Stream for 30 days.
